title: Children at home
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in a psychiatric assessment unit at 23:00. Mr Ellis, 35, has schizophrenia and was brought in by police after being found confused in a park. He is calmer now.

As you are assessing him, he says his children, aged 4 and 7, are "at home on their own". He says their mother is "away", but can't say where, and gives you his home address.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Contact the police to ask them to check on the children's safety now.
options.brief: Young children alone at night need an immediate safety check.
options.detailed: If the children are alone, they are at immediate risk. The police can attend straight away and involve children's social care. Acting promptly matters more than establishing every detail first.

options.text: Ask him calmly for more details about the children.
options.brief: More information helps those responding, without delaying the call.
options.detailed: He may be able to tell you whether a neighbour or relative is with them, or how long they have been alone. This helps the police and social care, and can be done while the call is made.

options.text: Ask a nurse to phone his home number to see whether anyone answers.
options.brief: An unanswered or answered call doesn't tell you the children are safe.
options.detailed: This might seem a quick check, but young children may not answer, and even if someone does, a phone call can't establish whether they are safe and supervised. It shouldn't replace or delay a police check.

options.text: Assume his statement is part of his illness until you can confirm it.
options.brief: The cost of being wrong is too high.
options.detailed: His statement could be affected by his illness, but if it's true, two young children are alone at night. You must act on the possibility.

options.text: Wait until the morning, when the children's social care offices are open and can visit.
options.brief: Far too slow for an immediate risk.
options.detailed: There is an out-of-hours social care service, and the police can act now. Waiting until morning could leave young children alone overnight.

options.text: Ask him to phone a neighbour to check on the children.
options.brief: Relies on an unwell man and an unknown neighbour for a child's safety.
options.detailed: A neighbour may help, but relying on him to arrange it, without any professional check, may leave the children unsafe.

options.text: Leave a note for the day team to follow up.
options.brief: Delays action on an immediate risk.
options.detailed: The day team will need to know, but leaving it until then is far too slow.

options.text: Inform the on-call psychiatrist, and record what he told you.
options.brief: Seniors need to know, and the record matters for safeguarding.
options.detailed: Your senior should be told about a serious safeguarding concern, and a clear record of what he said, when, and what you did supports the safeguarding process.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you act immediately on a possible risk to children, even when the information comes from an unwell parent.
explanation.keyDetails: Two young children may be alone at night. Their father is unwell and in hospital. Their mother's whereabouts are unknown.
explanation.reasoning: [A] gets an immediate safety check, [B] gathers helpful details, and [H] informs your senior and records it. The distractors delay ([C], [E], [G]), dismiss the risk ([D]), or rely on an unreliable arrangement ([F]).
explanation.competing: [D] is the trap: his statement may be affected by his illness, but you can't take that risk with young children.

references.title: Working together to safeguard children
references.note: Acting immediately when a child may be at risk of significant harm.

references.title: Protecting children and young people: the responsibilities of all doctors
references.note: Doctors' responsibilities to protect children, including children of adult patients.
